c.tagline: Mediterranean beaches, nightlife, and startup energy.

emergency.note: Fire is 102 and 112 works from mobiles; English-speaking operators are common.

hood_landmark.Florentin: graffiti-covered lanes at the heart of the city's street-art and bar scene
hood_landmark.Neve Tzedek: the Suzanne Dellal Centre for Dance amid restored historic lanes
hood_landmark.Jaffa (Yafo): Old Jaffa's ancient port, clock tower and flea market
hood_landmark.Rothschild (Lev Ha'ir): Rothschild Boulevard's UNESCO-listed White City Bauhaus architecture
hood_landmark.Ramat Aviv: ANU - Museum of the Jewish People on the Tel Aviv University campus

avoid.reason: Generally safe; follow local security guidance and rocket-alert procedures; usual petty-crime caution

hood_desc: Florentin is Tel Aviv's gritty, artsy district full of street art, workshops, and dive bars, buzzing with a young, bohemian crowd of artists, students, and night owls who love a raw creative edge. It suits budget-minded travelers who want authentic nightlife over polish.

Neve Tzedek is the citys oldest and most charming quarter, with restored Bauhaus and Ottoman-era homes on quiet cobbled lanes, boutiques, and cafes. It draws romantic, design-loving visitors and well-heeled couples seeking a picturesque, upscale village feel.

Jaffa (Yafo) is an ancient port town of stone alleys, a famous flea market, mosques, churches, and a mixed Arab-Jewish community, blending history with trendy galleries and restaurants. It appeals to culture seekers and foodies who want atmosphere and old-world character.

Rothschild (Lev Ha'ir) is the leafy, central heart of the city along Rothschild Boulevard, lined with Bauhaus architecture, banks, startups, cafes, and nightlife. It fits first-time visitors and business travelers wanting to be walkable to everything.

Ramat Aviv is an affluent, leafy residential district north of the Yarkon River, home to Tel Aviv University, the Eretz Israel and Palmach museums, and a major upscale mall. It suits families, academics, and quieter travelers who prefer calm suburban comfort over the downtown buzz.

water.note: Tap water meets high standards and is officially recommended by the Ministry of Health.

transit.pay: Get a Rav-Kav smart card (an anonymous card costs 5 NIS, loaded at machines, kiosks or tourist info centers) or tap a contactless credit card/Apple Pay at the validators. A single ride (with a 90-minute transfer window) costs about 8 NIS (~$2.20).
transit.hours: Light rail and buses run roughly 5am-midnight; nearly all transit, including trains, pauses for Shabbat from Friday afternoon to Saturday evening, with limited free weekend bus lines filling the gap.

transit.m: Israel Railways train to Tel Aviv (Savidor Center/HaShalom), ~15-20 min, does not run on Shabbat
Public bus (line 445) to central Tel Aviv, ~40-60 min

food.name: Hummus
food.desc: A warm plate of chickpea puree swirled with tahini, olive oil and paprika, topped with whole chickpeas or ful and wiped up with fresh pita. A morning food here.

places.name: Abu Hassan
places.note: The most famous hummus in Israel; order the triple and arrive before 10:30am or miss out.

places.name: Shlomo & Doron
places.note: Outdoor tables on a cobbled lane at the edge of Carmel Market; running since 1937.

places.name: Hummus HaCarmel
places.note: Market institution with fast turnover and hummus still warm from the pot.

food.name: Sabich
food.desc: Iraqi-Jewish Shabbat breakfast in a pita: fried aubergine, hard-boiled egg, hummus, tahini, chopped salad, pickled mango amba and a hit of chilli.

places.name: Sabich Tchernichovsky
places.note: Widely called the best sabich in the city; a counter with a permanent queue.

places.name: Sabich Frishman
places.note: Long-standing rival stand; generous amba and a good pickle bar.

places.name: Carmel Market sabich stands
places.note: Several stalls along the market do a quick, cheap version to eat walking.

food.name: Shakshuka
food.desc: Eggs poached in a spiced tomato and pepper stew, brought to the table in the cast-iron pan with bread for mopping. Breakfast, lunch or a late-night fix.

places.name: Dr. Shakshuka
places.note: Tripolitan-Libyan kitchen that built its name on the dish; giant pans, low prices.

places.name: Benedict
places.note: Breakfast served around the clock, with several shakshuka variations.

places.name: Cafe Puaa
places.note: Mismatched vintage furniture and a much-loved green shakshuka.

food.name: Bourekas
food.desc: Flaky Balkan pastries filled with salty cheese, potato or spinach, sold by weight and traditionally served with a hard-boiled egg and pickles.

places.name: Turkish Bourekas
places.note: A few doors into the shuk from Allenby; trays come out hot all morning.

places.name: Leon and Sons Bourekas
places.note: Old-school bakery doing the classic cheese and potato shapes correctly.

places.name: Yom Tov Delicatessen
places.note: Balkan deli with bourekas, pickles and salads to build a whole meal.

food.name: Malabi
food.desc: Silky milk pudding set with cornflour, flooded with rose or raspberry syrup and scattered with coconut and peanuts. Eaten from a cup on the street.

places.name: Malabi Dizingof
places.note: Small counter with a long list of toppings; the modern take locals actually queue for.

places.name: Carmel Market malabi stalls
places.note: Classic rosewater version for a few shekels, eaten standing in the crowd.

places.name: Jaffa flea market carts
places.note: Evening carts around the flea market serve it cold after dinner.

food.name: Falafel
food.desc: Herb-green chickpea fritters fried to order and stuffed into pita or laffa with salad, tahini, pickles and fried aubergine. Refills of salad are usually free.

places.name: Falafel HaKosem
places.note: The city's benchmark; balls fried on demand and a free one handed over while you wait.

places.name: Falafel Gabai
places.note: Neighbourhood stand going decades, favoured for its crisp shell and salad bar.

places.name: Falafel Razon
places.note: Fast, cheap and always busy with office workers at lunchtime.

food.name: Gazoz
food.desc: Sparkling water built to order with house-fermented syrups, foraged herbs, fruit and flowers. A revived Levantine soda now a Tel Aviv signature.

places.name: Cafe Levinsky 41
places.note: The tiny shop that started the gazoz revival; the maker builds each glass by hand.

places.name: Teder.fm
places.note: Courtyard bar and radio station pouring herbal sodas and spiked versions.

places.name: Levinsky Market spice shops
places.note: Several stalls now mix their own syrups; taste before you choose.

food.name: Limonana
food.desc: Lemonade blitzed with fresh mint and ice into a pale green slush. Invented as an Israeli ad campaign and now the default drink of a hot Tel Aviv afternoon.

places.name: Carmel Market juice stands
places.note: Blended in front of you from lemons and mint stacked on the counter.

places.name: Sarona Market
places.note: Indoor food hall with several juice bars, useful when the shuk is too hot.

places.name: Tayelet beach kiosks
places.note: Sand-side kiosks pour it all day; the classic pairing with a swim.

landmarks: Old Jaffa
An ancient port city of stone alleys, artist studios, and clocktower views over the Mediterranean, one of the world's oldest ports.
Tel Aviv Port (Namal)
A revitalized wooden boardwalk along the sea with cafes and sunset views, popular for waterfront photography.
Rothschild Boulevard
A leafy central boulevard lined with restored Bauhaus 'White City' buildings, the UNESCO-listed architectural signature of Tel Aviv.
Carmel Market (Shuk HaCarmel)
A bustling open-air market bursting with colorful produce, spices, and street food, ideal for vibrant candid shots.
Tel Aviv Beach Promenade
A long sandy shoreline with a lively boardwalk (tayelet), offering classic Mediterranean beach-city skyline photos.
Neve Tzedek
Tel Aviv's oldest neighborhood, known for its charming low-rise historic houses, boutique shops, and picturesque lanes.
Azrieli Center Towers
A trio of distinctive circular, triangular, and square skyscrapers that dominate Tel Aviv's skyline, an unmistakable modern landmark.
Habima Square & Theatre
The plaza in front of Israel's national theatre, featuring a striking outdoor amphitheater and modern public art.
Independence Hall
The modest building where Israel's independence was declared in 1948, a compact but historically iconic site.
HaTachana (The Old Railway Station)
A restored 19th-century train station complex turned pedestrian promenade of shops and restaurants near the beach.

train.note: No international trains run from Israel: the land borders with Lebanon and Syria are closed and there is no passenger rail link to Jordan or Egypt. Domestically, Israel Railways connects Tel Aviv (Savidor/HaHagana/Hashalom stations) with Jerusalem, Haifa, Be'er Sheva and Ben Gurion Airport; note trains do not run on Shabbat (Fri evening to Sat evening).

bus.note: There are no scheduled international through-coaches from Tel Aviv. To reach Jordan you travel to a land border (Sheikh Hussein/Jordan River in the north or the Allenby/King Hussein Bridge) and pick up onward transport, often via organised shuttles such as Abraham Tours; Egypt is reached via the Taba crossing near Eilat. Bring your passport and check current crossing status. Long-distance domestic coaches are run by Egged.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferries operate from Israel in 2026 - Haifa and Ashdod handle cargo and cruise ships only. During periods when flights are disrupted, ad-hoc charter ferries to and from Limassol (Cyprus) have run, but these are not a regular service - check locally before relying on one.

half.name: Zarqa
half.blurb: Industrial Jordanian city near Amman, known for its manufacturing and trade.

half.name: Gaza

half.name: Irbid

half.name: Russeifa
